quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Vocabulary of set-up and running cost, screens, colour wastage and short runs in a processing mill.

questions.q: Which of these is a running cost of a dyeing or printing machine rather than a set-up cost?
options: Wages of workers standing idle during a changeover
Electricity and gas consumed while the fabric is being processed
The minimum chemicals needed to start a batch
questions.explain: Running cost is incurred per metre while the machine works: labour on it, electricity, gas, depreciation. Idle wages, start-up chemicals and screen washing all belong to the changeover, i.e. set-up cost.

questions.q: A set-up cost is incurred once per order and does not depend on the length of the run.
questions.explain: The Rs 5,500 changeover is the same whether the order is 1,000 m or 10,000 m, which is why short runs are so much dearer per metre.

questions.q: In the lecture's example, conventional costing finds the average cost per metre by:
options: Dividing the set-up cost by the longest order
Charging each order its own set-up plus Rs 1 per metre
Dividing total cost of both orders by total metres of both orders
Taking the marketing charge of Rs 3 per metre
questions.explain: Conventional costing pools everything: (2 × 5,500 + 11,000) ÷ 11,000 m = Rs 2 per metre for both orders. Charging each order its own set-up is the ABC approach.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in the lecture as part of a rotary-printing changeover?
options: Removing and washing the screens, blades and drum
Changing blades if the fabric width changes
Re-engraving the screens for the next design
questions.explain: Screens are engraved once per design in the screen department; the changeover on the machine involves removing and washing screens, blades and drum, the back cloth and blade changes for width.

questions.q: Why do designs with more colours suffer more testing wastage at the rotary machine?
options: They use more fabric per metre
They must be checked at high speed for the colours to look sharp, and have more setting problems
Dark colours cost more per kg
questions.explain: The lecture notes that few-colour designs can be checked at slow speed with little wastage, while many-colour designs need high speed so colours become sharp enough to judge, and more screens means more setting problems.

questions.q: According to the lecture, about 4–5 screens out of 12 typically give an unsatisfactory shade and have to be washed and readjusted.
questions.explain: This is one of the department's observations; each readjusted screen wastes a further 5–6 kg of colour.

questions.q: Roughly how much colour does the lecture say is wasted at every changeover, before any screen readjustment?
questions.explain: At least 10–12 kg is lost at each changeover; readjusted screens add 5–6 kg each, and residual colour is left in the drum because the quantity needed is hard to estimate.

questions.q: The two components of a screen's cost named in the lecture's table are:
questions.explain: Each screen is filled (about Rs 1,400) and engraved (Rs 1,300–1,900 depending on width), giving roughly Rs 3,000 of labour per screen on average.

questions.q: What does the lecture say about vat dyes?
options: They are cheap and need one process
They are costly and need two processes
They are used only for printing
questions.explain: Vat dyes are expensive and require two processes, and dyeing has its own unavoidable wastage of colour and cloth.

questions.q: Over what life does the accounting department depreciate a screen, and why is this a problem?
options: 1,000 m — screens are written off too fast
65,000 m — real runs of 1,000–2,000 m never reach it, so the books fill with useless screen inventory
65,000 m — this matches typical run lengths
questions.explain: A 65,000 m life assumes the design will be repeated many times; with 1,000–2,000 m runs most screens are used once, so their cost stays on the books as 'inventory' while the order looks profitable.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How set-up, running and screen costs behave as run length, colours and width change.

questions.q: Under ABC, the cost of an order in the processing department is:
options: Set-up cost + running cost per metre × metres
questions.explain: ABC charges each order its own set-up plus the running cost for its length: 5,500 + 1 × 1,000 = Rs 6,500 for order A. Average cost × metres is the conventional method.

questions.q: A department's set-up cost is Rs 5,500 per order and the running cost is Rs 1 per metre. What is the ABC cost per metre of a 1,000 m order?
questions.explain: (5,500 + 1,000) ÷ 1,000 = Rs 6.50 per metre — more than double the Rs 3 marketing charges.

questions.q: If the run length of an order is doubled, the set-up cost per metre:
questions.explain: Set-up per metre = set-up ÷ metres, so doubling the metres halves it; the running cost per metre is unchanged.

questions.q: Screen cost per metre for a design is given by which expression?
options: Screen cost per screen × metres ÷ colours
Screen cost per screen × number of colours ÷ run length
questions.explain: Each colour needs a screen, so total screen cost = cost per screen × colours, and dividing by the metres printed gives cost per metre: 6,249 × 4 ÷ 400 = Rs 62.49.

questions.q: At a fixed run length, screen cost per metre is directly proportional to the number of colours in the design.
questions.explain: In the table, at 400 m the cost per metre goes 62.49 → 124.98 → 187.47 for 4, 8 and 12 colours: each extra screen adds the same amount per metre.

questions.q: From the screen cost table, as screen width increases from 1280 mm to 2800 mm, the engraving cost per screen:
questions.explain: Filling is a constant Rs 1,400; engraving rises with width from Rs 1,300 to Rs 1,900. The Rs 1,500–25,000 figures are the total screen cost ranges.

questions.q: Colour wastage: 12 colours each lose 11 kg at changeover, 5 screens are readjusted at 5 kg each, and 3 kg per colour is left in the drum. How many kg of colour are wasted in total?
questions.explain: 132 + 25 + 36 = 193 kg. Multiply by the average colour price to get the rupee loss (Rs 9,650 at Rs 50 per kg).

questions.q: Making one colour takes 10–15 minutes. For a 12-colour design the colour-kitchen time before printing is about:
questions.explain: 12 colours × 10–15 min = 120–180 min, i.e. 2–3 hours — the lecture quotes 3 hours. This is time the order must pay for whatever its length.

questions.q: Which cost does NOT fall per metre when the run length of a printing order increases?
options: Dye cost of the colour actually printed on each metre
Setting wastage of fabric per metre
questions.explain: Colour consumed on the fabric is a true running cost, proportional to metres. Screens, changeover wastage and setting wastage are per-order costs that get spread thinner on a longer run.

questions.q: A screen cost Rs 6,249 and is depreciated over 65,000 m. What depreciation does the accounts charge per metre, to three decimals?
questions.explain: 6,249 ÷ 65,000 = Rs 0.096 per metre — a tiny charge compared with the Rs 3.12 per metre the same screen really costs on a 2,000 m run.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Orders A and B, screen cost per metre and colour wastage worked through with numbers.

questions.q: Two orders of 1,000 m and 10,000 m each need a Rs 5,500 set-up; running cost is Rs 1 per metre. What average cost per metre does conventional costing give?
questions.explain: Total cost = 11,000 + 11,000 = Rs 22,000 over 11,000 m = Rs 2.00 per metre.

questions.q: Order A is 1,000 m, charged at Rs 3 per metre, with a Rs 5,500 set-up and Rs 1 per metre running cost. What is A's profit under ABC? (Give a loss as a negative number.)
questions.explain: Revenue 3,000 − cost (5,500 + 1,000) = −3,500: a loss of Rs 3,500, although conventional costing shows a Rs 1,000 profit.

questions.q: Order B is 10,000 m at Rs 3 per metre, with a Rs 5,500 set-up and Rs 1 per metre running cost. What is B's profit under ABC?
questions.explain: 30,000 − 15,500 = Rs 14,500, against Rs 10,000 conventionally: B had been carrying half of A's set-up.

questions.q: With a Rs 5,500 set-up, Rs 1 per metre running cost and a charge of Rs 3 per metre, what is the minimum order length at which an order breaks even?
questions.explain: Each metre contributes 3 − 1 = Rs 2 towards the set-up; 5,500 ÷ 2 = 2,750 m. Any shorter order loses money at Rs 3.

questions.q: A design needs 12 screens at Rs 12,000 each and the run is 1,000 m. What is the screen cost per metre?
questions.explain: 12 × 12,000 = Rs 144,000 of screens; ÷ 1,000 m = Rs 144 per metre, before any wages, electricity or wastage.

questions.q: Average screen cost is Rs 6,249. What is the screen cost per metre for an 8-colour design run for 2,000 m, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 6,249 × 8 = 49,992; ÷ 2,000 = Rs 25.00 per metre, matching the table.

questions.q: Using an average screen cost of Rs 6,249, what is the screen cost per metre of a 12-colour design on a 20,000 m run, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 74,988 ÷ 20,000 = Rs 3.75 per metre — 50 times less than the Rs 187.47 for the same design on 400 m.

questions.q: 193 kg of colour is wasted on a 12-colour design at an average Rs 50 per kg. What is the colour wastage in rupees?
questions.explain: 193 × 50 = Rs 9,650, the figure in the lecture's worksheet. On a 1,000 m run that is almost Rs 10 per metre.

questions.q: A 2400 mm screen costs Rs 1,400 to fill and Rs 1,600 to engrave. What is the labour on the screen?
questions.explain: 1,400 + 1,600 = Rs 3,000, the 'about Rs 3,000 of labour per screen' the lecture quotes. Rs 5,664–22,450 is the table's total screen cost range for that width.

questions.q: Colour wastage of Rs 9,650 plus screens of Rs 74,988 are incurred on a 12-colour design run for 2,000 m. What is the combined cost per metre, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 84,638 ÷ 2,000 = Rs 42.32 per metre, before running cost, fabric wastage or any profit.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Pricing and planning decisions in a printing and dyeing mill once set-up costs are traced.

questions.q: Marketing charges a flat Rs 3 per metre for processing. A customer sends a stream of 1,000 m orders. What is the likely result?
options: Each order loses Rs 3,500 because the set-up alone costs Rs 5,500
The orders earn more than the 10,000 m orders
questions.explain: ABC shows a 1,000 m order costs Rs 6,500 but brings in Rs 3,000. The conventional sheet's Rs 1,000 profit is an illusion created by pooling the set-ups.

questions.q: Which pricing policy best reflects the ABC findings for a processing department?
options: One flat rate per metre for all orders
A set-up charge per order plus a lower rate per metre
A higher rate per metre for long orders
Free processing for orders under 1,000 m
questions.explain: Charging the set-up per order and the running cost per metre makes each customer pay for what their order causes; long orders become cheaper per metre, as they should.

questions.q: A planner can run a 4-colour design or a 12-colour design on rotary #4 for a 400 m sample order. Which is cheaper in screens and why?
options: The 12-colour one, because more colours mean sharper checking
The 4-colour one, at about Rs 62 per metre of screens instead of Rs 187
They cost the same because the run length is the same
The 12-colour one, because dark colours are cheaper
questions.explain: Screen cost per metre is proportional to colours: 4 × 6,249 ÷ 400 = Rs 62.49 against Rs 187.47 for 12 colours, and the 4-colour design can be checked at slow speed with less wastage.

questions.q: Because screens are depreciated over 65,000 m, a 1,000 m order of a new design shows almost no screen cost in the accounts.
questions.explain: At Rs 6,249 ÷ 65,000 m the charge is under Rs 0.10 per metre, so the order looks profitable while the unused screen value sits on the balance sheet as inventory.

questions.q: The costing office wants to reduce colour wastage at changeover. Which observation from the lecture points to the largest avoidable item?
options: 4–5 of 12 screens give a wrong shade and are readjusted, wasting 5–6 kg each
questions.explain: Readjusted screens are a quality failure that can be reduced by better colour matching before printing; the 10–12 kg of changeover loss and drum residue are harder to avoid.

questions.q: A customer asks for a quotation for 400 m of a 12-colour print. Using the lecture's figures (Rs 6,249 per screen), the screen cost alone is about:
questions.explain: 12 × 6,249 ÷ 400 = Rs 187.47 per metre. Rs 62.49 is for 4 colours at 400 m and Rs 74.99 for 12 colours at 1,000 m.

questions.q: Which change would reduce the cost per metre of a printing order the most for a fixed design?
options: Increasing the run length so the screens and changeover wastage are spread over more metres
questions.explain: Screens, changeover wastage and setting wastage are all per-order costs; only run length dilutes them. Wider screens and dark colours cost more, not less.

questions.q: A mill owner says: 'Our printing orders all show a profit in the monthly accounts, so why is cash short?' Which explanation fits the lecture?
options: The accounts are counting screen cost as inventory while cash was spent on screens that will never be reused
Colour wastage is a non-cash item
questions.explain: Cash has gone on screens and wasted colour for short runs, but the books charge only Rs 0.10 per metre of screen depreciation and carry the rest as an asset, so profits look fine while cash disappears.

questions.q: Dyeing has no essential wastage of colour, so it should always be preferred to printing.
questions.explain: The lecture states that dyeing has its own essential wastage of colour and cloth, and vat dyeing needs two processes; the choice depends on the product, not on wastage alone.

questions.q: A planner groups several small orders of the same design and colours into one long run. Which costs fall per metre as a result?
options: Only the running cost per metre
Screen cost, changeover colour wastage and setting wastage per metre
None, because each customer still pays Rs 3
questions.explain: One changeover and one set of screens now serve all the metres, so every per-order cost is spread thinner. Running cost per metre is unchanged.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step problems and common mistakes across set-up, running, screen and colour costs.

questions.q: Set-up Rs 5,500, running Rs 1 per metre. What charge per metre, to two decimals, would give a 1,000 m order a 20 % margin on cost?
questions.explain: ABC cost = Rs 6,500; × 1.2 = Rs 7,800; ÷ 1,000 m = Rs 7.80 per metre, compared with the Rs 3 flat charge.

questions.q: A student says order A's loss under ABC is Rs 1,000 − Rs 6,500 = −Rs 5,500. What has gone wrong?
options: Profit is revenue minus cost, so it should be Rs 3,000 − Rs 6,500 = −Rs 3,500, not the conventional profit minus the ABC cost
questions.explain: Rs 1,000 is the conventional profit, not revenue; mixing the two systems double-deducts cost. Revenue 3 × 1,000 = Rs 3,000 less ABC cost Rs 6,500 gives a Rs 3,500 loss.

questions.q: Under conventional costing orders A (1,000 m) and B (10,000 m) show profits of Rs 1,000 and Rs 10,000. Under ABC they show −Rs 3,500 and Rs 14,500. What is the total profit under each system — give the difference between the two totals.
questions.explain: Both systems total Rs 11,000; ABC only moves Rs 4,500 of profit from A to B. A costing system redistributes cost, it never creates or destroys it.

questions.q: A 12-colour design uses 12 screens at Rs 6,249 each. Over how many metres must the design be printed in total for the screen cost to fall to Rs 1 per metre?
questions.explain: 74,988 ÷ metres = 1 gives 74,988 m — more than the 65,000 m depreciation life, and far beyond typical 1,000–2,000 m runs.

questions.q: Screens cost Rs 12,000 each. Which of these jobs has the lowest screen cost per metre?
questions.explain: Cost per metre = 12,000 × colours ÷ metres: Rs 120, Rs 48, Rs 14.40 and Rs 24 respectively. The 12-colour job wins because 10,000 m dilutes its screens; the tempting 4-colour 2,000 m job costs Rs 24.

questions.q: Screens cost Rs 12,000 each. By how many rupees per metre is a 4-colour design on 2,000 m dearer in screens than a 12-colour design on 10,000 m, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 4 × 12,000 ÷ 2,000 = Rs 24.00; 12 × 12,000 ÷ 10,000 = Rs 14.40; difference Rs 9.60 per metre. Run length matters more than colour count.

questions.q: Colour wastage for a 12-colour design is 193 kg. If the average colour price rises from Rs 50 to Rs 60 per kg, by how many rupees does the wastage cost rise?
questions.explain: 193 × 10 = Rs 1,930; total wastage goes from Rs 9,650 to Rs 11,580.

questions.q: Reducing readjusted screens from 5 to 2 (at 5 kg each) on a 12-colour design saves 15 kg of colour.
questions.explain: 3 fewer screens × 5 kg = 15 kg, worth Rs 750 at Rs 50 per kg; the 132 kg of changeover loss and 36 kg drum residue are unaffected.

questions.q: The lecture quotes light, medium and dark colours at Rs 30, 45 and 100 per kg. The worksheet uses an average of Rs 50. Which statement is right?
options: Rs 50 is the simple average of the three prices
Rs 50 is a rounded working figure; the simple average of the three prices is about Rs 58
Rs 50 is the price of medium colours
Rs 50 is the cost of residual colour only
questions.explain: (30 + 45 + 100) ÷ 3 = Rs 58.33. The worksheet input of Rs 50 is a working assumption you can edit; a design heavy in dark colours would cost much more.

questions.q: A mill processes 11,000 m a month in 11 orders of 1,000 m each. Set-up is Rs 5,500 per order and running cost Rs 1 per metre. If the same 11,000 m came as a single order, how much would be saved?
questions.explain: Eleven orders need 11 set-ups (Rs 60,500); one order needs one (Rs 5,500). The saving is 10 × 5,500 = Rs 55,000; running cost of Rs 11,000 is the same either way.
